Newly hatched chicks of the White-crowned pigeon, Patagioenas leucocephala, emerge from the egg weighing just 14.3 grams [Ww0 = 14.3 grams], a modest initial mass typical of altricial columbid nestlings. This neonatal body mass represents the starting point for a rapid growth trajectory that sees hatchlings more than double their weight within the first week under consistent brooding. The incubation period, which lasts approximately 14 days [ab = approximately 14 days], unfolds at a nest temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C], a thermal regime maintained by the attentive biparental care characteristic of the genus. During this embryonated egg stage, the developing chick relies entirely on yolk reserves; the albumen-buffered embryo undergoes organogenesis within the calcareous eggshell before pipping. Once hatched, the nestling enters a period of intensive parental provisioning that fuels its somatic development toward the adult body dimensions observed in breeding populations.

Adult body mass in the White-crowned pigeon exhibits modest sexual dimorphism, with females reaching a maximum recorded wet weight of 236.7 grams [Wwi = 236.7 grams] while males attain a slightly heavier ultimate wet weight of 237.9 grams [Wwi = 237.9 grams]. These values were derived from large-scale field surveys conducted across the species' Caribbean and Floridian range, where breeding individuals were captured and weighed during the nesting season. The slight difference in body mass between the sexes is consistent with patterns observed in other members of the Columbidae family, where males often carry marginally greater structural size. This dimorphism is thought to reflect divergent selective pressures: males invest energy in territorial defense and courtship displays, while females channel resources into egg production and the energetic demands of incubation. Importantly, these adult masses are achieved over a period of sustained growth, with young birds gradually accumulating body condition through the juvenile and subadult stages before reaching their definitive size.

Under controlled thermal conditions approximating the species' active metabolic state at 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], researchers measured a basal oxygen consumption rate of 242 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 242 milliliters of oxygen per hour] for resting adults. This value provides a baseline for understanding the energetic costs of daily maintenance in a bird that forages extensively on the fruits of tropical hardwoods and mangroves. The relatively modest metabolic rate compared to other pigeons of similar body size likely reflects adaptations to a frugivorous diet, which is relatively low in protein and requires extended gut passage times for efficient nutrient extraction. Resting metabolic rates were determined via flow-through respirometry on post-absorptive individuals during the inactive phase of their daily cycle, a standard protocol that minimizes the confounding effects of digestive activity and locomotion. These data contribute to a growing comparative dataset on columbid energetics across a latitudinal gradient.

The reproductive biology of the White-crowned pigeon is characterized by a slow, K-selected life history, with females laying two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch] and typically producing a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year]. This extremely low annual fecundity is among the most constrained of any North American columbid and appears to be linked to the species' dependence on spatially patchy and temporally unpredictable fruit resources. The energetic investment per egg is substantial, as each egg represents a significant fraction of the female's body mass, and the incubation and brooding periods impose continuous metabolic demands on both parents. Field studies conducted across the Florida Keys and Bahamian islands consistently report this monogamous single-brood strategy, with very few documented cases of double-brooding even under favorable conditions. Nest predation by raccoons and rats further depresses overall reproductive output, reinforcing the premium placed on adult survival.

Nestlings achieve fledging, defined as the successful departure from the nest and the attainment of sustained flight, at 15 days after hatching [tx = 15 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This relatively brief nestling period is followed by a longer phase of parental dependency during which the fledgling learns foraging skills and refines its flight abilities. Sexual maturity, marked by the onset of gonadal activity and the capacity to participate in courtship and breeding, is reached at 46 days after hatching [tp = 46 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C].
